questions.enonce_markdown:
Carefully examine two instances in the fourth Gospel which justify the fact that Jesus is the Bread of life.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** "I am the bread of life" (John 6:35) is the first of the "I am" sayings with a predicate in the Fourth Gospel. Two instances in John 6 justify the claim: the feeding of the five thousand and the discourse on the bread of life that follows. The Last Supper, though differently told in John, can be added as a third point.

**Instance 1: the feeding of the five thousand (6:1-15).**
- A large crowd followed Jesus because of the signs that he did for the sick. Jesus tests Philip about where bread can be bought, and Andrew points to a boy with five barley loaves and two fish.
- Jesus takes the loaves, gives thanks and distributes them, and the people eat as much as they want. Twelve baskets of fragments are collected, which shows abundance and that nothing is wasted.
- The people say, "This is indeed the prophet who is to come into the world" (6:14), and they wish to make Jesus king.
- This sign shows that Jesus can satisfy hunger and that his provision is generous. It recalls the manna given through Moses and points beyond bread for the body to a deeper hunger.

**Instance 2: the discourse in the synagogue at Capernaum (6:25-59).**
- The crowd asks for a sign like the manna in the wilderness (6:30-31). Jesus answers that it was not Moses but the Father who gave the bread from heaven, and that "the bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world" (6:32-33).
- He then declares, "I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty" (6:35).
- He explains that the manna did not prevent death, but whoever eats the living bread will live for ever (6:48-51). The bread is Jesus himself, given for the life of the world.
- Believing in him and coming to him is therefore the way to eternal life, and Jesus promises to raise up those who believe on the last day (6:40).

**How the two instances justify the title.** The sign gives a visible demonstration of Jesus' power to feed, and the discourse interprets the sign: Jesus gives not only physical food but the life that comes from God. Together they show that he sustains and gives life, as bread does, but with a life that does not end.

**Reaction.** Some of the listeners find the teaching hard, and many of his disciples leave him (6:60-66), while Peter confesses that Jesus has "the words of eternal life" (6:68). This shows that accepting the title requires faith.

**Conclusion.** The feeding of the five thousand and the discourse at Capernaum together justify the claim that Jesus is the Bread of life: he provides abundantly for the needs of people and gives eternal life to those who believe in him.
